questions.q: Which organelle is the site of protein synthesis?
questions.why: Ribosomes translate mRNA into polypeptides.

questions.q: Which feature is found in prokaryotic cells?
questions.why: Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles; their ribosomes are 70S.

questions.q: The resolution of a light microscope is limited by…
questions.why: Resolution is about half the wavelength used; electrons have much shorter wavelengths.

questions.q: An eyepiece graticule must be calibrated using…
questions.why: The stage micrometer's known divisions give the value of each graticule unit at that magnification.

questions.q: Which structure is found in the cytoplasm of prokaryotic cells?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): two thirds of weaker candidates chose endoplasmic reticulum; prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles.

questions.q: Which organelle contains hydrolytic enzymes responsible for breaking down cellular waste and ingested pathogens?
questions.why: Lysosomes maintain an acidic interior with acid hydrolases that digest macromolecules, old organelles, and engulfed foreign matter.

long.q: In an electron micrograph a mitochondrion measures 18 mm. Its actual length is 3 µm. Calculate the magnification of the image.
scheme: A1: magnification = 18 000 ÷ 3 = × 6000

questions.q: Which bond joins two α-glucose molecules in maltose?
questions.why: A condensation reaction forms an α-1,4 glycosidic bond.

questions.q: What gives cellulose its strength?
o: Hydrogen bonds between parallel chains of β-glucose forming microfibrils
questions.why: Alternate β-glucose units are inverted, giving straight chains that hydrogen-bond together.

questions.q: Which level of protein structure is the sequence of amino acids?
questions.why: The primary structure determines how the chain folds.

questions.q: Why is water a good solvent?
o: It is polar, so ions and polar molecules dissolve
questions.why: Its δ+ and δ− regions surround charged and polar particles.

questions.q: Which statement about cellulose is correct?
o: It is an unbranched chain of β-glucose, held in microfibrils by hydrogen bonds
It is a branched chain of α-glucose
Its chains coil into a helix
It is a polymer of fructose
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many thought cellulose is branched or coils into a helix; that describes starch (amylopectin and amylose).

questions.q: Which statement about triglycerides is correct?
o: They are non-polar and insoluble in water
questions.why: Examiners (2023): half of weaker candidates believed triglycerides are polar.

questions.q: Which bond forms between the glycerol molecule and fatty acids in a triglyceride?
questions.why: Condensation reactions between each –OH group of glycerol and the –COOH group of a fatty acid produce ester bonds with the elimination of water.

long.q: Describe the structure of cellulose and explain how it suits its role in plant cell walls.
scheme: B1: β-glucose monomers joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds, alternate ones rotated 180°
B1: long straight chains held together by many hydrogen bonds into microfibrils
B1: giving high tensile strength, so the wall resists bursting when the cell is turgid

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor…
o: binds to the active site, competing with the substrate
binds elsewhere and changes the active site
questions.why: Raising substrate concentration can overcome it; Vmax is unchanged.

questions.q: A low Km means the enzyme has…
questions.why: Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax; low Km means it reaches it at low concentration.

questions.q: Why are immobilised enzymes useful?
o: They work faster than free enzymes always
They can be reused and are more stable, and the product isn't contaminated
questions.why: Fixing enzymes in beads makes separation and reuse easy.

questions.q: In an enzyme-catalysed reaction, the rate rises as substrate concentration increases but then levels off. Why does it level off?
o: The substrate has been used up
The enzyme has been denatured by the extra substrate
All the active sites are occupied at any moment, so enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor
The product acts as a competitive inhibitor
questions.why: At high substrate concentration the enzyme is saturated: adding more substrate cannot form enzyme–substrate complexes any faster, so the rate reaches Vmax.

questions.q: How does a competitive inhibitor affect Vmax and Km?
questions.why: A high enough substrate concentration out-competes the inhibitor, so Vmax can still be reached; but more substrate is needed to reach half Vmax, so Km rises.

long.q: Explain how a non-competitive inhibitor affects the Vmax and the Michaelis–Menten constant (Km) of an enzyme.
scheme: B1: it binds to a site other than the active site (allosteric site)
B1: changing the shape of the active site, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form
B1: Vmax is lower; adding more substrate does not overcome it
B1: Km is unchanged (the affinity of the remaining active enzymes is the same)

questions.q: In the fluid mosaic model, what makes the membrane fluid?
o: Phospholipids that move within the layer
questions.why: Phospholipids move laterally; cholesterol regulates fluidity.

questions.q: Facilitated diffusion uses…
o: channel or carrier proteins, down a concentration gradient
questions.why: It is passive, but needs proteins for polar or charged molecules.

questions.q: Water potential of pure water is…
questions.why: Ψ of pure water is 0 kPa; solutes make it negative.

questions.q: Where is cholesterol found in a cell surface membrane?
o: Between the phospholipid tails, with its OH group near the heads
questions.why: Examiners (2023): three fifths of weaker candidates thought cholesterol only occurs between the heads.

questions.q: Two neighbouring plant cells have water potentials of −400 kPa (cell A) and −700 kPa (cell B). What happens?
o: Water moves from B to A, because B has more solute
Water moves from A to B, down the water potential gradient
There is no net movement, because both values are negative
Water moves from B to A, because B has the lower water potential
questions.why: Water moves by osmosis from a higher (less negative) to a lower (more negative) water potential: −400 kPa is higher than −700 kPa, so water moves from A into B.

long.q: A plant cell is placed in pure water. Explain, in terms of water potential, what happens to the cell.
scheme: B1: pure water has a higher (less negative) water potential than the cell (0 kPa)
B1: water moves into the cell by osmosis, down the water potential gradient, through the partially permeable membrane
B1: the cell becomes turgid; the cell wall stops it bursting

questions.q: In which stage do chromosomes line up on the equator?
questions.why: Spindle fibres attach to centromeres and align chromosomes at metaphase.

questions.q: When is DNA replicated?
questions.why: DNA synthesis happens in the S phase before mitosis.

questions.q: What is the role of telomeres?
o: Protect chromosome ends from losing genes during replication
questions.why: Repeated non-coding sequences are lost instead of genes.

questions.q: Which statement about mitosis is correct?
o: Daughter cells are the same size as the parent
Semi-conservative DNA replication happens during mitosis
The nuclear envelope breaks down during prophase
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates thought DNA replication is part of mitosis (it is in interphase) or forgot the nuclear envelope breaks down in prophase.

questions.q: At which stage of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles of the spindle?
questions.why: During anaphase, cohesin proteins break down and kinetochore spindle fibres pull separated sister chromatids to opposite poles.

questions.q: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative because…
o: each new molecule has one original strand and one new strand
it happens in half the cells
questions.why: Shown by the Meselson–Stahl experiment.

questions.q: Which enzyme joins Okazaki fragments?
questions.why: Ligase seals the gaps in the lagging strand.

questions.q: During translation, tRNA anticodons pair with…
questions.why: Complementary base pairing places the right amino acid.

questions.q: A substitution mutation may have no effect because…
o: the genetic code is degenerate (several codons per amino acid)
questions.why: A different codon can still code for the same amino acid.

questions.q: Which sugar is found in ATP?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): nearly three fifths of weaker candidates said deoxyribose.

questions.q: What enzyme synthesises an mRNA transcript from a DNA template strand during transcription?
questions.why: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter, unwinds the helix, and synthesises complementary pre-mRNA from 5' to 3'.

scheme: B1: hydrogen bonds between bases break and the double helix unwinds (helicase)
B1: each strand acts as a template
B1: free nucleotides pair with complementary bases (A–T, C–G)
B1: DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides, so each new molecule has one old strand and one new strand

questions.q: What drives water up the xylem?
o: Transpiration pull, with cohesion and adhesion
questions.why: Evaporation from leaves creates tension that pulls a continuous column of water up.

questions.q: Sucrose is loaded into phloem sieve tubes by…
o: co-transport with H⁺ via companion cells
questions.why: Companion cells pump H⁺ out; sucrose re-enters with H⁺ through co-transporters.

questions.q: Xerophytes reduce water loss by…
o: sunken stomata, rolled leaves and thick cuticles
questions.why: These trap humid air and reduce the surface exposed.

questions.q: Water moving through the apoplast pathway in a root:
o: moves only by osmosis through membranes
moves by mass flow through cell walls
questions.why: Examiners (2023): over half of candidates said the apoplast pathway does not involve mass flow.

questions.q: What causes the mass flow of phloem sap from a source to a sink?
o: Active pumping of sap by the companion cells along the whole sieve tube
A hydrostatic pressure gradient: sucrose loading at the source lowers water potential so water enters, and unloading at the sink has the opposite effect
questions.why: Water following sucrose by osmosis raises hydrostatic pressure at the source and lowers it at the sink, so sap flows down the pressure gradient, in either direction depending on where sources and sinks are.

questions.q: The Bohr effect means that high CO₂ concentration…
questions.why: Oxygen is released more readily where respiration is high.

questions.q: What starts each heartbeat?
questions.why: The SAN starts a wave of excitation; the AVN delays it before the ventricles contract.

questions.q: Tissue fluid forms because at the arterial end of a capillary…
o: hydrostatic pressure is greater than the osmotic pull
questions.why: Fluid is forced out; most returns at the venous end.

questions.q: In what form is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
o: Hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻), mostly in the plasma
Carbonic acid molecules in the plasma
questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells converts CO₂ and water to H₂CO₃, which dissociates to H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; the HCO₃⁻ diffuses into the plasma in exchange for Cl⁻ (the chloride shift).

questions.q: During the cardiac cycle, what causes the atrioventricular valves to close?
o: Pressure in the atria rises above pressure in the ventricles
Pressure in the ventricles rises above pressure in the atria as the ventricles contract
Pressure in the ventricles falls below pressure in the aorta
An impulse from the SAN contracts the valve tissue
questions.why: Valves open and close passively because of pressure differences; when ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, blood pushes the AV valve flaps shut, preventing backflow into the atria.

long.q: Explain the Bohr shift and why it is useful in actively respiring tissues.
scheme: B1: high carbon dioxide concentration lowers the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen (curve shifts right)
B1: CO₂ forms carbonic acid, and H⁺ ions bind to haemoglobin forming haemoglobinic acid
B1: so more oxygen is released (unloaded) where it is needed for respiration

questions.q: What is the role of cartilage in the trachea?
questions.why: C-shaped rings stop the trachea collapsing.

questions.q: Goblet cells…
questions.why: Cilia then sweep the mucus upwards.

questions.q: Which tissue lines the trachea and bronchi and produces mucus?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): 'endothelium' was a wrong choice: that term is only used for blood vessels.

questions.q: Which feature of the alveoli most directly shortens the diffusion distance for oxygen?
o: A surfactant that coats their inner surface
The large number of alveoli in each lung
Walls made of a single layer of thin, flattened (squamous) epithelial cells next to capillary walls
questions.why: Thin squamous epithelium and thin capillary walls mean oxygen crosses only about two cells; the large number of alveoli increases surface area rather than shortening the distance.

questions.q: What is the role of elastic fibres in the walls of the alveoli?
o: They stretch during inhalation and recoil during exhalation, helping to push air out
They contract to close the airways
They keep the alveoli permanently open, like cartilage
questions.why: Elastic fibres stretch as the alveoli fill and then recoil, helping to expel air; they are passive, unlike smooth muscle, and do not hold airways open as cartilage does.

questions.q: Which organism causes malaria?
questions.why: Plasmodium is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes.

questions.q: How does penicillin kill bacteria?
o: It stops cell wall synthesis, so cells burst
It blocks ribosomes in human cells
questions.why: Without strong walls, bacteria burst by osmosis as they grow.

questions.q: How is cholera transmitted?
o: Through water or food contaminated with faeces containing Vibrio cholerae
questions.why: Treatment of sewage and clean drinking water prevent it.

questions.q: Which pathogen causes tuberculosis (TB), and how is it usually transmitted?
o: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, in airborne droplets from an infected person
questions.why: TB is a bacterial disease spread when infected people cough or sneeze; it spreads more easily in overcrowded housing.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics not effective against HIV?
o: HIV is too small for antibiotics to reach
HIV has a thick cell wall that antibiotics cannot penetrate
Viruses have no cell walls, ribosomes or metabolism of their own for antibiotics to target; they use the host cell's machinery
questions.why: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures or processes such as cell wall synthesis or bacterial ribosomes; a virus has none of these to disrupt.

long.q: Explain how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic.
scheme: B1: a random mutation gives a bacterium resistance (e.g. a gene for an enzyme that breaks down the antibiotic)
B1: when the antibiotic is used, resistant bacteria survive and non-resistant ones die (selection pressure)
B1: resistant bacteria reproduce and pass on the allele, also by horizontal gene transfer on plasmids

questions.q: Which cells produce antibodies?
questions.why: Activated B cells divide and differentiate into plasma cells.

questions.q: Passive immunity is…
questions.why: No memory cells are made, e.g. antibodies across the placenta.

questions.q: Monoclonal antibodies are produced by…
questions.why: They are identical and target one specific antigen.

questions.q: Why is the secondary immune response to a pathogen faster and larger than the primary response?
o: Antibodies from the first infection remain in the blood for life
The pathogen is weaker the second time
Plasma cells from the first infection keep dividing
Memory cells made during the first response recognise the antigen and divide rapidly
questions.why: Memory B and T cells persist after the primary response; on re-infection they quickly divide, producing many plasma cells and more antibody, often before symptoms appear.

questions.q: What is the main role of T helper cells in the immune response?
o: They produce antibodies against the antigen
They release cytokines that stimulate B cells to divide and become plasma cells, and activate other immune cells
They kill infected body cells directly
questions.why: T helper cells coordinate the response through cytokines; plasma cells make antibodies, T killer cells destroy infected cells, and phagocytes engulf pathogens.

long.q: Distinguish between active and passive immunity, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: active: the person's own immune system makes antibodies after meeting an antigen
B1: example: vaccination, or recovering from an infection
B1: passive: antibodies are given from outside; no memory cells form, so it is short-lived
B1: example: antibodies across the placenta or in breast milk, or an injection of antibodies

questions.q: Where does the Krebs cycle take place?
questions.why: Glycolysis is in the cytoplasm; link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix.

questions.q: What is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation?
questions.why: Oxygen combines with electrons and H⁺ to form water.

questions.q: A respiratory quotient (RQ) near 0.7 suggests the substrate is…
questions.why: Carbohydrate 1.0, protein about 0.9, lipid about 0.7.

questions.q: In aerobic cellular respiration, where does the Krebs (citric acid) cycle take place?
questions.why: The matrix houses soluble enzymes for the link reaction and Krebs cycle; oxidative phosphorylation occurs on the inner membrane.

questions.q: In anaerobic conditions, yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂. What is the main purpose of this?
o: To regenerate NAD so that glycolysis can continue
To store energy in ethanol for later use
questions.why: Without oxygen, reduced NAD cannot be reoxidised by the electron transport chain; reducing ethanal to ethanol reoxidises it, so glycolysis can keep making its net 2 ATP.

long.q: Explain how ATP is produced by oxidative phosphorylation.
scheme: B1: reduced NAD/FAD release electrons to the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane
B1: energy from electron flow pumps H⁺ into the intermembrane space
B1: H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis)
B1: driving ADP + Pi → ATP
B1: oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water

questions.q: Where does the light-dependent stage happen?
questions.why: Photosystems and the electron transport chain are in the thylakoids.

questions.q: Which enzyme fixes CO₂ in the Calvin cycle?
questions.why: Rubisco combines CO₂ with RuBP.

questions.q: A limiting factor is…
o: the factor that controls the rate because it is in shortest supply
questions.why: Increasing it increases the rate until another factor limits.

questions.q: In the light-independent stage of photosynthesis (Calvin cycle), which enzyme fixes CO₂ to ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP)?
questions.why: RuBisCO (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase) catalyses the primary carbon fixation reaction yielding 3-PGA.

questions.q: A photosynthesising plant is suddenly placed in the dark. What happens to the concentrations of GP and RuBP in its chloroplasts?
questions.why: Without light there is no ATP or reduced NADP to reduce GP to triose phosphate, so GP builds up; RuBP is still used in fixing CO₂ but cannot be regenerated, so it falls.

long.q: Describe the light-independent stage of photosynthesis (the Calvin cycle).
scheme: B1: CO₂ combines with RuBP, catalysed by rubisco
B1: forming two molecules of GP
B1: GP reduced to triose phosphate using ATP and reduced NADP
B1: most TP regenerates RuBP, using ATP

questions.q: Which hormone increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct?
questions.why: ADH inserts aquaporins, making urine more concentrated.

questions.q: Homeostasis mainly works by…
questions.why: A change triggers a response that reverses it.

questions.q: Guard cells open stomata by…
o: taking in K⁺, lowering water potential, then water enters and they swell
questions.why: Turgid guard cells bend apart because of uneven wall thickness.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT normally found in the glomerular filtrate of a healthy kidney?
questions.why: Plasma proteins are too large to pass through the basement membrane during ultrafiltration; small molecules such as glucose, urea and ions pass into the filtrate.

questions.q: How does glucagon raise blood glucose concentration?
o: It increases the uptake of glucose by muscle cells
It converts glucose into glycogen in liver cells
It is released by β cells and acts directly on glycogen
It binds to receptors on liver cells and, via the second messenger cAMP, activates enzymes for glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis
questions.why: Glucagon from α cells cannot enter the cell; binding to its receptor starts a cAMP signalling cascade that activates enzymes breaking down glycogen and making glucose from other compounds.

long.q: Explain how blood glucose concentration is lowered after a meal.
scheme: B1: β cells in the islets of Langerhans detect the rise and secrete insulin
B1: insulin binds to receptors on liver and muscle cells
B1: more glucose transporters (GLUT4) in membranes, so more glucose uptake
B1: glucose converted to glycogen (glycogenesis)
B1: negative feedback

questions.q: What causes the depolarisation in an action potential?
o: Na⁺ rushing in through voltage-gated channels
questions.why: Repolarisation then follows as K⁺ leaves.

questions.q: Myelination speeds up conduction by…
o: saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier
questions.why: Action potentials jump from node to node.

questions.q: Which plant hormone stimulates stomatal closure in drought?
questions.why: ABA triggers K⁺ loss from guard cells.

questions.q: What maintains the resting potential of a neurone at about −70 mV?
o: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, and the membrane is more permeable to K⁺, which diffuses out
Acetylcholine binds to the axon membrane
questions.why: More positive charge leaves than enters through the pump, and K⁺ leaking out through open channels leaves the inside negative relative to the outside.

questions.q: Why can a nerve impulse cross a synapse in one direction only?
o: Neurotransmitter is released only from the presynaptic neurone, and receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane
The synaptic cleft is too wide for ions to cross backwards
Myelin blocks transmission in the other direction
Acetylcholinesterase is found only in the presynaptic knob
questions.why: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are in the presynaptic knob and the receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane, so the signal can only pass from pre- to postsynaptic neurone.

long.q: Explain how a nerve impulse is transmitted across a cholinergic synapse.
scheme: B1: action potential arrives; Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ enters the presynaptic knob
B1: vesicles fuse and release acetylcholine by exocytosis
B1: ACh diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
B1: Na⁺ channels open, depolarising the membrane
B1: acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh

questions.q: Crossing over happens in…
questions.why: Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange sections.

questions.q: A chi-squared test compares…
questions.why: It tests whether differences from the expected ratio are due to chance.

questions.q: Epistasis is…
o: one gene affecting the expression of another gene
questions.why: It changes expected dihybrid ratios.

questions.q: A plant heterozygous for two unlinked genes (AaBb) is crossed with a plant that is aabb. What is the expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring?
questions.why: The AaBb parent makes four gametes (AB, Ab, aB, ab) in equal numbers by independent assortment; the aabb parent only gives ab, so each gamete type gives a different phenotype.

questions.q: Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A carrier woman (XᴴXʰ) and an unaffected man (XᴴY) have a son. What is the probability that the son has haemophilia?
questions.why: A son gets Y from his father and one of his mother's two X chromosomes, so there is a 1 in 2 chance he inherits Xʰ. 1/4 is the chance that any child is an affected son.

long.q: In a dihybrid cross between two plants heterozygous for both genes (AaBb × AaBb), state the expected phenotypic ratio and explain what a significantly different result could suggest.
scheme: B1: genes on different chromosomes assort independently
B1: a different ratio may suggest linkage (genes on the same chromosome)
B1: test with chi-squared

questions.q: The Hardy–Weinberg equation is p² + 2pq + q² = 1. What is 2pq?
questions.why: p² = AA, 2pq = Aa, q² = aa.

questions.q: Genetic drift has the largest effect in…
questions.why: Chance changes in allele frequency matter more when numbers are small.

questions.q: What is genetic drift?
o: Random changes in allele frequency, strongest in small populations
questions.why: The founder effect and bottlenecks are examples.

questions.q: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 16% of individuals show the recessive phenotype. What is the frequency of heterozygotes?
questions.why: q² = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 0.6; heterozygotes = 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48. 0.36 is p² and 0.84 is everyone with the dominant phenotype.

questions.q: Which sequence describes allopatric speciation?
o: Mutation in one individual immediately produces a new species
Populations are separated by a geographical barrier; different selection pressures and genetic drift change their gene pools until they can no longer interbreed
Populations in the same area become reproductively isolated by behavioural changes
Individuals acquire useful characteristics during their lives and pass them on
questions.why: Allopatric speciation needs geographical isolation first; reproductive isolation in the same area is sympatric speciation, and passing on acquired characteristics is not how evolution works.

questions.q: Simpson's index of diversity is higher when…
o: there are many species with similar numbers
questions.why: Diversity includes both richness and evenness.

questions.q: Which are the three domains?
questions.why: Domains are the highest rank in classification.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of taxonomic ranks, largest first?
o: Kingdom, domain, class, phylum, order, genus, family, species
Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom, domain
Domain, phylum, kingdom, class, family, order, genus, species
questions.why: There are three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya.

questions.q: A sample contains 10 individuals of species A, 6 of species B and 4 of species C. Using D = 1 − Σ(n/N)², what is Simpson's index of diversity?
questions.why: N = 20, so Σ(n/N)² = 0.5² + 0.3² + 0.2² = 0.25 + 0.09 + 0.04 = 0.38, and D = 1 − 0.38 = 0.62. 0.38 is the result if you forget to subtract from 1.

questions.q: Why are viruses not placed in any of the three domains?
o: They are too small to see with a light microscope
They are not made of cells and cannot carry out metabolism or reproduce outside a host cell
questions.why: The domains classify cellular organisms; viruses are acellular, so they are classified separately by features such as their nucleic acid type (DNA or RNA).

questions.q: What does PCR do?
o: Makes many copies of a DNA sequence
questions.why: Cycles of denaturing, annealing primers and extending with Taq polymerase.

questions.q: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by…
questions.why: Negatively charged DNA moves towards the anode; small fragments travel faster.

questions.q: What do restriction enzymes do?
o: Cut DNA at specific base sequences
questions.why: DNA ligase joins fragments; sticky ends help them pair.

questions.q: Why is the same restriction enzyme used to cut both the plasmid and the DNA containing the gene to be inserted?
o: So that both pieces of DNA are the same length
So that the gene is copied many times
So that both have complementary sticky ends that base-pair, before DNA ligase joins the sugar–phosphate backbones
So that the plasmid cannot be taken up by bacteria
questions.why: One restriction enzyme leaves matching single-stranded overhangs on both molecules, so the gene and plasmid base-pair by hydrogen bonding and ligase then seals them.

questions.q: To make human insulin in bacteria, the gene is usually made from insulin mRNA using reverse transcriptase rather than cut from human chromosomal DNA. Why?
o: The cDNA made from mRNA has no introns, and bacteria cannot remove introns
Reverse transcriptase also adds a promoter that bacteria recognise
Bacteria can only use RNA, not DNA
questions.why: Mature mRNA has already been spliced, so cDNA copied from it codes for insulin with no introns; bacteria have no splicing machinery to remove them from a eukaryotic gene.

long.q: Describe how PCR is used to amplify a sample of DNA.
scheme: B1: heated to about 95 °C to separate the strands
B1: cooled to about 55 °C so primers anneal
B1: heated to about 72 °C; Taq polymerase extends the strands
B1: cycle repeated, doubling the DNA each time
